newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: FOCUS - Slovenia clamps down on foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Slovenia clamps down on foreign investment.

text.p: Slovenia's central bank clamped down on foreign trading activity on Tuesday, sending shares into a tailspin that analysts said could knock up to 50 percent off prices and sully the market's growing reputation.
A central bank said a ruling forcing international investors to use special trading accounts, operated by selected Slovenian banks, was aimed at regulating foreign investment.

It succeeded in ending a foreign-funded bull run that had taken the blue-chip SBI 40 percent higher since the start of the year. On Tuesday the SBI finished 140.59 points, or 8.46 percent, down at 1,521.83.
"We wanted to organise foreign portfolio investment," Darko Bohnec, head of central bank operations, told Reuters.

The first Slovenian banks received notification of the ruling late on Friday but were unsure how to interpret the move. Austrian-owned Creditanstalt, which has a high proportion of foreign customers, heard late on Monday and was the prime mover behind Tuesday's sell-off.
"Such a restriction is unexpected and shameful for Slovenia and may ruin foreign and domestic trust in the securities' market," Creditanstalt trader Karmen Korbun said.

Only banks with full licences can operate the new accounts, preventing half of Slovenia's 28 banks from accepting foreign funds for share investments. They have 30 days from February 7 to establish the accounts. Cash transactions through them will be limited to 250,000 tolars ($1,655) a month.

Under existing regulations the central bank already keeps a tight rein on the amount of foreign currency in circulation. Banks said the details of the latest decree and their likely impact on day-to-day business remained vague.

"We got instructions that each foreign exchange inflow will have to be balanced by placing the same amount abroad, which would be virtually impossible to do in large amounts," Creditanstalt's Korbun said.

"This is a shock to the market. The procedure on how these accounts have to be established is not clear and it may last several weeks before the situation clears up ," said Aleksander Simon, an analyst at Nova Ljubljanska Banka.
Market participants forecast a bumpy road ahead for the Ljubljana market, until Tuesday the darling of investors in the emerging economies of eastern Europe.

Since the beginning of this year foreign money has accounted for about half of turnover. New listings like drug firms Lek and Krka and food producers Droga and Kolinska have attracted international investors in droves.
"I see the index falling 30 to 50 percent from yesterday's levels if the Bank of Slovenia does not change its position (and) I do not expect (that) to happen very soon," one trader said.

"It all depends on how banks and foreign investors react. At the moment things are still very unclear but if foreigners retreat from the market prices could fall to their September level," said Toni Apollonio, an analyst at A Banka.
September marked the start of the Ljubljana's most recent bull run. Since then the SBI index has soared some 70 percent.
